text:
Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years, someone in education announces that handwriting is finished. Keyboards have won, the argument goes, so teachers should stop spending precious hours on loops and ligatures and give children laptops instead. Joined-up writing, also called cursive, is the easiest target. It looks old-fashioned, it is hard to master, and many adults abandon it the moment they leave school. Why not let it go?

Because the case for dropping it is weaker than it sounds. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting, and teach it properly. It supports fluency, spelling, and thinking itself. It gives children a tool they will use for decades. And the arguments against it, once examined, mostly describe bad teaching of cursive, not a flaw in cursive itself.

Start with what handwriting is for. It is easy to treat it as a purely mechanical skill, a way of getting words onto paper. But for a seven-year-old, writing is not mechanical at all. Every letter must be recalled, shaped, and placed. If that process is slow and effortful, it consumes working memory that the child needs for the real work of writing: choosing words, building sentences, holding an idea in mind long enough to finish it. Researchers in this area have long noted that children who write automatically produce longer, better-organised compositions than children who struggle with letter formation, even when their ideas are equally good. Handwriting fluency is not the opposite of creativity. It is what frees creativity up.

Joined-up writing, taught well, is the fastest route to that fluency. When letters are written separately, the pen leaves the page after every character. Each lift is a small break in rhythm, and each re-landing is a fresh chance to misplace the next letter. Joined writing turns a word into a single movement. The hand learns the word as a pattern, not as a string of disconnected marks. Anyone who has watched a confident cursive writer will recognise the difference: the pen moves continuously and the words arrive almost without effort. Print can be quick too, but it tends to plateau at a lower speed, and children who rely on it often reach secondary school writing too slowly to keep up with note-taking and timed exams.

There is also a link with spelling that deserves more attention than it gets. Because a joined word is produced as one motor sequence, common letter strings such as "ing", "tion", and "ough" become physical habits as well as remembered facts. Teachers of children with spelling difficulties have long used cursive for this reason. The hand carries some of the memory. This is not a miracle cure, and the evidence base is better for some claims than others, but the principle is sound: the more channels through which a child encounters a word, the more securely it is learned.

The most interesting evidence concerns what handwriting does to learning more broadly. Several studies comparing handwritten and typed note-taking have found that writing by hand tends to produce better conceptual understanding. The likely reason is that handwriting is slower, which forces the writer to compress and rephrase, while typists are tempted to transcribe word for word. Neuroimaging work has also suggested that handwriting activates areas of the brain involved in reading and language more strongly than typing does, particularly in children. Some of this research is still developing and should not be oversold. But the direction of travel is consistent, and it runs against the assumption that the keyboard is simply a faster pen. Writing by hand is a different cognitive act, and a primary school is exactly the place to build it.

Now consider the practical objection: nobody writes by hand any more. This is simply untrue. Children write by hand every day in school, in every subject, and they will continue to do so in the exam hall for the foreseeable future. Adults write shopping lists, birthday cards, forms, margin notes, and signatures. A signature is itself a joined-up flourish that most people produce without thinking. The idea that handwriting is vanishing mistakes a change in proportion for a disappearance. Yes, we type more. We also still need to write by hand, and we need to do it legibly and without strain. A child who cannot is at a real disadvantage, and it is a disadvantage that falls hardest on children from homes with fewer resources, who may not have a keyboard at home to compensate.

That point about fairness matters. Dropping cursive in favour of "just use a device" sounds modern, but it quietly assumes every child has equal access to technology and equal practice with it. Schools are where that assumption gets corrected. A pencil and paper are the great equaliser. Teaching handwriting well is one of the few things a school can do that costs almost nothing and benefits every child regardless of background.

Another objection is that print is clearer, so why force children through the extra step of joining? There is a respectable version of this argument. Some education systems teach a simple, print-based style first and introduce joins later, and some research suggests that a hybrid style, with print-like letters and a few easy joins, can be just as fast and legible as full cursive. Fair enough. But notice what that argument concedes. It does not say joins are pointless. It says the form of joined writing should be sensible. The right response is to teach a clean, modern, joined style, not to abandon joining altogether. Elaborate looped capitals and decorative flourishes can go. The continuous, flowing movement that makes joined writing efficient should stay.

The strongest argument against cursive is that it is hard, and that some children, especially those with motor difficulties or dyslexia, find it harder still. This is true, and it deserves a serious answer. But the answer is support, not removal. Teachers already adapt tasks for children who struggle with reading, number, or attention. Handwriting is no different. Some pupils will need more time, simpler letterforms, or a keyboard as a supplement. That is an argument for flexibility within a curriculum that still teaches joining, not for deleting it for everyone. If anything, children with motor difficulties often benefit from the continuous movement of cursive, because it reduces the number of separate starts the hand must make. Plenty of specialist teachers recommend it for exactly that reason.

It is also worth saying something about time. Critics sometimes imagine cursive eating up hours that could go to coding or reading. In practice, handwriting instruction in a good primary school is brief and frequent: ten minutes a day, built into the routine, with the skill then used constantly across every other subject. The cost is small. The return, a lifetime of legible and comfortable writing, is large. And a child who writes fluently will complete every other written task faster, which hands time back to the rest of the curriculum.

Finally, there is something to be said for the less measurable side of the question. Joined-up handwriting is a craft. Children take quiet pride in a neat page, and the physical act of writing carefully teaches patience and attention in a way that tapping keys does not. We do not defend this on sentimental grounds alone, because the cognitive and practical arguments are strong enough. But a school day with no space for slow, careful, hand-made work would be poorer for it. Childhood already offers plenty of screens. A pencil is a refreshing change.

So what should schools actually do? Teach handwriting explicitly and early, starting with correct letter formation in print as children learn to read, then introducing joins once the basic shapes are secure, ideally by the age of seven or so. Choose a simple, consistent, joined style across the whole school so that children are not confused by different models from different teachers. Practise little and often, with proper attention to pencil grip, posture, and paper position, which are the unglamorous foundations of comfortable writing. Give extra support where it is needed rather than lowering the bar for everyone. And teach typing as well, because the goal is not to choose between the pen and the keyboard but to give children both.

That last point is important. The debate is too often framed as tradition against progress, as though defending handwriting meant rejecting technology. It does not. A child should leave primary school able to type competently and to write by hand fluently. These skills are complements, not rivals. The keyboard is better for long drafts and editing. The pen is better for quick notes, for thinking on paper, for exams, and for the many small moments in life when no device is at hand. A literate adult is comfortable with both.

The people who want to abandon joined-up writing are right about one thing: it should not be taught as a rigid, joyless drill in an ornate historical style. But the remedy for poor teaching is better teaching. Handwriting that flows supports fluent composition, secure spelling, deeper learning, and fair access for every child. It costs little and lasts a lifetime. Primary schools should keep the joins.
